title: Twentieth-century analytic philosophy
audience: a college student in a philosophy degree program, or an adult studying the same material on their own
purpose: Trace analytic philosophy from Frege, Russell and Moore through Wittgenstein's Tractatus, the logical positivists and the verification principle, Carnap and Quine on ontology and analyticity, ordinary language philosophy and the later Wittgenstein, to the revival of metaphysics with modal logic, Kripke and Lewis.
primary_reading: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Analytic Philosophy (free)

weeks.2: Russell and Moore: the revolt against idealism
weeks.4: The Vienna Circle and the verification principle
weeks.6: Carnap: linguistic frameworks and internal and external questions
weeks.7: Quine: "Two Dogmas of Empiricism" and analyticity
weeks.8: Quine: naturalized epistemology and ontological relativity
weeks.9: The later Wittgenstein: meaning as use and rule-following
weeks.10: Ordinary language philosophy: Austin and Ryle
weeks.11: The return of metaphysics: modal logic, Kripke and Lewis
weeks.12: Analytic philosophy today: naturalism and its critics

blocks.deliverable: Explain Russell's paradox and why it mattered.
Apply the verification principle to five sentences.
Explain Carnap's distinction between internal and external questions.
Week 7 midterm; reconstruct Quine's case against analyticity.
Write a three-page essay on the Carnap-Quine debate.
Submit the project; take an unseen 120 minute final in week 14.

project: History of a debate: write a 2,500-word paper tracing one debate (verificationism and its fall, the analytic-synthetic distinction, or the Carnap-Quine debate about ontology) from its origin to its present state, reconstructing the key arguments and assessing which side has the better of it today.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
